newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech central bank move needs follow-up - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech central bank move needs follow-up - analysts.

text.p: The Czech National Bank (CNB) silenced its critics on Thursday by intervening to support the crown, but analysts said further long-term measures must follow or the currency will continue to weaken.

After months of threats fell on deaf market ears, the CNB finally intervened on behalf of the crown after it fell about one percentage point when trading opened to a record low of 5.00 percent against its dollar/mark basket parity.
The CNB moved through two main waves of intervention, its first such move in over a year, to bring the crown back to about 3.4 percent on the depreciation side of basket parity.
But analysts said the effects of the intervention would be short-term at best, and warned the bottom could fall out from under the crown if the CNB did not take further action soon.

"The central bank has only so much in reserves and the Czech crown market, with so many Eurobond issues and players in London...is making it much harder for the CNB to control the crown," said John Vax, director of ING Barings Capital Markets.
"There is now a lot of expecation in the money market for a rate hike and there has been a massive selloff in the bond market...Even if it doesn't want to the market may force it to move," he added.
At the end of March, the CNB's foreign exchange reserves were almost unchanged from the month before at 11.7 billion.

In explaining the move, the CNB said the crown's fall was due to fluctuations of several foreign currencies. It did not elaborate, but some traders said foreign investors were getting nervous over some emerging market economies troubled by weak external position, such as Thailand.
"The CNB today intervened on the forex market with the aim of stabilising the crown's exchange rate," a CNB statement said. "If needed, the CNB is ready for further intervention."
The CNB did not reveal the amounts it had spent on reviving the crown, but analysts estimated it may have cost tens of millions of dollars in total.
While some analysts have said the crown is long-overdue for a devaluation, most said they did not expect such drastice action would be taken.

"When the short-term portfolio players begin to move out, this sort of thing (a weakening currency) happens. (But) I don't really think a devaluation of the crown is economically necessary," said Jonathan Garner of Flemings.

Analysts said it appeared as though the long-rumoured, but never confirmed, five percent central bank support level had set off the intervention. "The five percent band appears to be real," said one Frankfurt analyst.

"(But) I think the market feels that intervention by itself will not be able to sustain the sentiment. Reserves are not that high, so the market overall is still bearish about the currency," he added.
The CNB fixed the crown 3.4 percent weaker against the basket midpoint and in late afternoon activity, the crown remained steady at -3.3 percent.

The central bank has been threatening to act since February when the crown -- boosted by demand from a wave of nearly 50 billion crowns worth of crown-denominated Eurobond issues -- hit a record high of 5.51 percent on the appreciation side of basket parity.

Since then, the crown has fallen sharply driven by worries about the country's overall macroeconomic prospects and a widespread belief that the CNB would heed government calls for a relaxation of monetary policy to boost growth.
Last Thursday, however, the CNB ruled out any relaxation of monetary policy in the near term.

Thursday's intervention marked the first time it had actually entered the market to move the crown since February 1996 when the band within which the crown is fixed was widened to +/-7.5 percent from a previous +/-0.5 percent.
But analysts said the market had grown to such an extent following the Eurobond craze that the market, if not satisfied with the CNB's actions, could bully the crown further.
"The CNB is really subject to the whims of the market and if its reserves begin to become depleted, then it could become a feeding frenzy (on the market)," Vax said.
